q: Which tissue components define endometriosis histologically?
x: Endometriosis is endometrial glands and stroma outside the uterus, usually with hemosiderin-laden macrophages from old bleeding; glands alone are not enough, and the ectopic tissue responds to cyclic hormones by bleeding.

w.Endometrial glands without stroma: Stroma is required for the diagnosis; isolated glands could be a mimic such as a metaplastic or neoplastic focus, and endometrial stroma gives the tissue its hormone-responsive bleeding.
w.Smooth muscle bundles and stroma: Smooth muscle with stroma describes myometrium or a leiomyoma; endometriosis contains no muscle bundles of its own, though it can induce reactive muscle thickening nearby.
w.Plasma cells and lymphoid follicles: Plasma cells in the stroma define chronic endometritis, an inflammatory lining disease linked to pelvic infections or an IUD, not to ectopic tissue.
w.Mucinous epithelium and ovarian stroma: Mucinous epithelium with ovarian-type stroma characterizes mucinous cystic neoplasms of the ovary, not the endometrial tissue found in endometriosis.

q: Which symptom triad is typical of endometriosis?
o: Postcoital bleeding, discharge and weight loss
Fever, cervical motion tenderness and discharge
Heavy periods, pressure and urinary frequency
x: Dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia and dyschezia result from cyclic bleeding and scarring of implants in the pelvis: painful periods, deep pain with intercourse and painful defecation, often with infertility, while the uterus stays normal in size.

w.Postcoital bleeding, discharge and weigh: This describes advanced cervical cancer, which bleeds after intercourse and can cause a watery discharge; endometriosis causes cyclic pain instead of bleeding from a friable mass.
w.Amenorrhea, galactorrhea and headache: This suggests a prolactinoma, in which excess prolactin suppresses GnRH and a pituitary mass compresses surrounding structures; it causes no pelvic pain.
w.Fever, cervical motion tenderness and di: This is pelvic inflammatory disease from ascending chlamydia or gonorrhea, an acute infection with purulent discharge rather than months of cyclic pain.
w.Heavy periods, pressure and urinary freq: This describes leiomyomas, whose bulk presses on the bladder and whose submucosal members cause bleeding; endometriosis does not usually enlarge the uterus.

q: Which condition produces a uniformly enlarged, boggy, globular uterus?
x: Adenomyosis places endometrial glands and stroma inside the myometrium, and the muscle thickens around them, so the whole uterus enlarges symmetrically and feels soft and tender with heavy, painful periods.

w.Endometriosis: Endometriosis lies outside the uterus on the ovaries and peritoneum, so the uterus itself stays normal in size and may be fixed in place by adhesions.
w.Leiomyoma: Fibroids are discrete, firm, whorled nodules that make the uterus asymmetric and lumpy rather than uniformly globular and boggy.
w.Endometrial polyp: A polyp is a small focal growth in the cavity causing irregular bleeding; it does not enlarge the uterine body.
w.Endometrial carcinoma: Endometrial carcinoma usually presents with postmenopausal bleeding and a normal or mildly enlarged uterus, without the diffuse, tender, globular enlargement of a thickened muscular wall.

pt.say: Label 5 marks adenomyosis, glands in the muscle that make a globular, tender uterus.

q: Which is the most common tumor in women?
x: Leiomyomas, benign estrogen-sensitive smooth muscle tumors, occur in a large majority of women by menopause, which makes them the most common tumor in women; they cause bleeding, pressure and infertility.

w.Endometrial carcinoma: Endometrial carcinoma is the most common gynecologic cancer, but it is far less common than fibroids, which are present in most women by menopause.
w.Serous cystadenoma: Serous cystadenomas are common benign ovarian tumors, yet they occur in a small fraction of women compared with uterine fibroids.
w.Cervical polyp: Cervical polyps are common benign growths of endocervical glands, but they are far less frequent than uterine leiomyomas.
w.Granulosa cell tumor: Granulosa cell tumors are rare sex cord-stromal ovarian neoplasms that secrete estrogen; their rarity contrasts with the extreme frequency of fibroids.

pt.say: The leiomyoma column opens with the fact that it is the most common tumor in women.

q: Which fibroid location most often causes heavy menstrual bleeding?
x: Submucosal fibroids bulge into the uterine cavity, stretch and ulcerate the lining and impair contraction, so they cause menorrhagia, intermenstrual bleeding and miscarriage out of proportion to their size.

w.Subserosal: Subserosal fibroids grow outward under the peritoneal surface, producing pressure on the bladder or bowel and sometimes a stalk, but they distort the lining little and bleed less.
w.Cervical: Cervical leiomyomas are uncommon and typically obstruct the canal or compress adjacent structures, rather than being the usual source of heavy periods.
w.Broad ligament: Broad ligament fibroids arise beside the uterus and can compress the ureter, but they lie outside the cavity and do not cause the lining to bleed.
w.Parasitic omental: A parasitic fibroid is a pedunculated subserosal tumor that has attached to the omentum and acquired its own blood supply; it is rare and does not bleed through the vagina.

pt.say: Label 2 shows the submucosal leiomyoma bulging into the cavity, the location that causes heavy bleeding.

o: Spindle cells, plasma cells and edema
x: Leiomyosarcoma is diagnosed when cytologic atypia, tumor cell necrosis and a high mitotic rate are assessed together, because mitoses alone occur in benign tumors of young women; these tumors are soft, hemorrhagic and necrotic.

w.Whorls, calcification and hyalinization: These are degenerative and architectural changes of benign leiomyomas, which are firm and whorled and may calcify; they signal a benign tumor.
w.Glands, stroma and hemosiderin: These are the components of endometriosis, in which old bleeding leaves hemosiderin-laden macrophages; they have nothing to do with a smooth muscle malignancy.
w.Papillae, atypia and psammoma bodies: This combination marks serous carcinoma, an epithelial tumor of atrophic endometrium with TP53 mutation, rather than a spindle cell sarcoma.
w.Spindle cells, plasma cells and edema: Plasma cells in stroma point to chronic endometritis, an inflammatory process; spindle cells with plasma cells do not define a malignancy.

pt.say: The leiomyosarcoma column lists atypia, necrosis and mitoses as the features that together define the malignancy.

q: What best predicts progression of endometrial hyperplasia to carcinoma?
x: Cytologic atypia, with enlarged rounded nuclei and prominent nucleoli, defines atypical hyperplasia (EIN), which frequently coexists with endometrioid carcinoma; hyperplasia without atypia progresses in only a small percentage.

w.Cystic gland dilation: Cystic dilation reflects retained secretions in glands and is common in benign hyperplasia, which carries a low risk of cancer.
w.Glandular crowding: Crowding is what defines hyperplasia in the first place and occurs in both low-risk and high-risk lesions, so it cannot predict the outcome.
w.Squamous morules: Squamous morules are small whorls of metaplastic squamous cells seen in some endometrioid lesions; they are a benign-appearing metaplasia, not a marker of malignant potential.
w.Stromal edema: Stromal edema is a nonspecific change in secretory or breakdown endometrium and carries no prognostic weight for cancer.

pt.say: The hyperplasia box says no atypia means low risk, so atypia is the finding that raises cancer risk.

q: Which tumor suppressor is lost early in type I endometrial carcinoma?
x: PTEN loss, which removes a brake on the PI3K growth pathway, is an early event in atypical hyperplasia and endometrioid carcinoma; germline PTEN mutation causes Cowden syndrome.

w.TP53: TP53 mutation is the early event in serous carcinoma, the type II tumor of atrophic endometrium, rather than in the estrogen-driven endometrioid tumors.
w.BRCA1: BRCA1 mutation predisposes to breast and ovarian cancer through defective homologous recombination and has no central role in endometrioid carcinoma.
w.RB1: RB1 loss is characteristic of retinoblastoma and osteosarcoma and is not a recognized early driver of type I endometrial carcinoma.
w.APC: APC loss starts the adenoma-carcinoma sequence of colorectal cancer; it is not an early event in endometrioid carcinoma.

pt.say: The type I pathway shows PTEN loss at the atypical hyperplasia step, an early event in endometrioid carcinoma.

q: Which gene mutation is an early, central event in serous endometrial carcinoma?
x: TP53 mutation appears at the intraepithelial carcinoma stage and drives chromosomal instability and aberrant p53 staining, so type II tumors are high grade and spread early.

w.PTEN: PTEN loss drives estrogen-dependent endometrioid carcinoma and hyperplasia; serous tumors arise in atrophic endometrium without this pathway.
w.BRCA1: BRCA1 is linked to breast and ovarian cancer, and although serous tumors of the pelvis can occur in carriers, it is not the central event in serous endometrial carcinoma.
w.RB1: RB1 normally restrains the G1 checkpoint and is disabled by HPV E7 in cervical disease, but it is not a defining event of serous endometrial carcinoma.
w.APC: APC mutations drive colorectal adenomas through disturbed Wnt signaling and are not central to serous endometrial carcinoma.

pt.say: The type II row shows TP53 mutation as the early, central event leading to serous carcinoma.

q: What is the precursor lesion of serous endometrial carcinoma?
x: Serous endometrial intraepithelial carcinoma is a TP53-mutated, surface-confined proliferation of malignant cells that can shed through the tubes and seed the peritoneum even without myometrial invasion.

w.Atypical hyperplasia (EIN): EIN is the precursor of estrogen-driven endometrioid carcinoma and carries PTEN loss, not the TP53 changes of the serous pathway.
w.Hyperplasia without atypia: Simple hyperplasia without atypia is a low-risk, progestin-responsive estrogen effect and has no direct link to the serous pathway.
w.Endometrial polyp: A polyp can harbor serous carcinoma, but it is a benign focal overgrowth rather than the defined intraepithelial precursor of the serous pathway.
w.Adenomyosis: Adenomyosis is endometrial tissue in the muscle wall and is not a premalignant lesion of the endometrial surface epithelium.

pt.say: The serous precursor box names serous endometrial intraepithelial carcinoma, abbreviated SEIC.

q: Which inherited syndrome links colorectal and endometrial cancer through mismatch repair loss?
x: Lynch syndrome is an autosomal dominant germline defect in MLH1, MSH2, MSH6 or PMS2; microsatellite instability predisposes to colorectal, endometrial, ovarian and urinary tract cancers.

w.Cowden syndrome: Cowden syndrome arises from germline PTEN mutation, giving hamartomas and breast, thyroid and endometrial cancer, but its tumors keep mismatch repair proteins.
w.Peutz-Jeghers syndrome: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, from STK11 mutation, causes mucocutaneous pigmentation and hamartomatous polyps with increased risk of breast, pancreatic and sex cord tumors.
w.Familial adenomatous polyposis: Familial adenomatous polyposis results from APC mutation and produces hundreds of colonic adenomas, with colon cancer nearly certain unless the colon is removed.
w.Li-Fraumeni syndrome: Li-Fraumeni syndrome results from germline TP53 mutation and causes sarcomas, breast cancer, brain tumors and adrenocortical carcinoma at young ages.

pt.say: The note under the type I row says mismatch repair defects are inherited in Lynch syndrome.

q: Which uterine tumor contains both malignant epithelium and malignant mesenchyme?
x: Carcinosarcoma, also called malignant mixed Müllerian tumor, is a biphasic tumor of postmenopausal women with TP53 mutations; the sarcomatous part is generally metaplastic change within a single carcinoma.

w.Leiomyosarcoma: Leiomyosarcoma is a pure malignant smooth muscle tumor without a carcinomatous component.
w.Endometrial stromal sarcoma: Endometrial stromal sarcoma is a pure mesenchymal malignancy resembling proliferative-phase stroma, with no malignant epithelial element.
w.Adenosarcoma: Adenosarcoma pairs benign glands with a malignant stromal component, the reverse of carcinosarcoma, in which both elements are malignant.
w.Leiomyoma: Leiomyoma is a benign smooth muscle tumor with a single cell population and no malignant epithelium or mesenchyme.

pt.say: The footnote places carcinosarcoma, the malignant mixed Müllerian tumor, with the aggressive p53-driven type II group.

q: Which drug acts as a partial estrogen agonist on the endometrium?
x: Tamoxifen blocks estrogen in breast cancer cells but stimulates the endometrium, causing polyps, hyperplasia and endometrial cancer; bleeding on tamoxifen needs endometrial sampling.

w.Raloxifene: Raloxifene is a modulator that antagonizes the breast and endometrium while helping bone, so it does not carry tamoxifen's risk of endometrial cancer.
w.Anastrozole: Anastrozole inhibits aromatase and lowers estrogen everywhere, so it atrophies rather than stimulates the endometrium.
w.Clomiphene: Clomiphene blocks estrogen feedback at the hypothalamus to induce ovulation; in the endometrium it is antiestrogenic and can thin the lining.
w.Fulvestrant: Fulvestrant is a pure estrogen receptor antagonist and degrader with no agonist effect, so it does not stimulate the lining.

pt.say: Tamoxifen is listed among the causes of unopposed estrogen effect at the start of the type I road.

q: Which exposure lowers the risk of endometrial carcinoma?
x: A combined oral contraceptive supplies a progestin every cycle, which opposes estrogen and thins the lining, and the protection lasts for years after stopping; pregnancy and progestin IUDs protect similarly.

w.Nulliparity: Nulliparity means fewer progesterone-dominant pregnancies and more uninterrupted cycles, which lengthens estrogen exposure and raises risk.
w.Obesity: Obesity raises risk because adipose aromatase converts androgens to estrogen, producing unopposed estrogen even when ovulation continues.
w.Late menopause: Late menopause extends the number of years of cycling and estrogen exposure, which raises the lifetime risk.
w.Estrogen-only therapy: Unopposed estrogen therapy given to a woman with a uterus causes hyperplasia and cancer, which is why a progestin is added.

pt.say: The protective box lists the combined oral contraceptive alongside progestin and pregnancy.

q: Which cell identifies chronic endometritis on biopsy?
x: Plasma cells in the endometrial stroma define chronic endometritis, which follows pelvic inflammatory disease, an IUD, retained tissue or tuberculosis and causes spotting and infertility.

w.Neutrophil: Neutrophils dominate acute endometritis, as after delivery or abortion with retained products, rather than the chronic form.
w.Eosinophil: Eosinophils suggest an allergic or parasitic process and are not the defining cell of chronic endometritis.
w.Foamy macrophage: Foamy macrophages accumulate in conditions such as xanthogranulomatous inflammation or lipid storage disease, not in the common forms of chronic endometritis.
w.Multinucleated giant cell: Giant cells form granulomas, as in tuberculous endometritis, a rare cause; the usual defining cell of chronic endometritis is the plasma cell.

q: Which event most often precedes Asherman syndrome?
x: Curettage, especially after pregnancy, scrapes away the basalis, and intrauterine adhesions replace it; the cavity cannot rebuild a lining, causing secondary amenorrhea and infertility with normal hormone levels.

w.Tubal ligation: Tubal ligation occludes the tubes without entering the uterine cavity, so it does not scar the endometrium.
w.Hysterosalpingography: Hysterosalpingography is a diagnostic dye study that shows adhesions as filling defects but does not cause them.
w.Colposcopy-directed biopsy: A cervical biopsy samples the cervix and does not disturb the endometrial basalis inside the uterine cavity.
w.Intrauterine insemination: Insemination passes a thin catheter through the cervix to deposit sperm and does not abrade the endometrium enough to scar it.

q: Which procedure shows the uterine cavity directly and permits polyp removal?
x: Hysteroscopy passes a camera through the cervix into the cavity, so the surgeon can see polyps, fibroids and adhesions and remove or biopsy them under direct vision.

w.Colposcopy: Colposcopy magnifies the cervix after acetic acid to target biopsies of cervical dysplasia; it does not enter the uterine cavity.
w.Diagnostic laparoscopy: Laparoscopy views the outside of the uterus, tubes, ovaries and peritoneum, which makes it the way to see endometriosis, but it cannot see inside the cavity.
w.Hysterosalpingography: Hysterosalpingography outlines the cavity and tubes with radiographic dye and can suggest polyps or adhesions, but it is an imaging study and cannot remove anything.
w.Transvaginal ultrasonography: Ultrasonography measures lining thickness and finds masses indirectly, but it gives no direct view and no tissue.

q: Danazol is used for endometriosis and which other disease?
x: Danazol is a synthetic androgen that suppresses gonadotropins to atrophy endometriosis and also raises hepatic synthesis of C1 esterase inhibitor, which prevents attacks of hereditary angioedema.

w.Polycystic ovary syndrome: PCOS involves androgen excess, so an androgenic drug would worsen hirsutism and acne; it is treated with weight loss, contraceptives and antiandrogens.
w.Prolactinoma: Prolactinomas are treated with dopamine agonists such as cabergoline, which shrink the lactotroph tumor; danazol has no such action.
w.Hypothyroidism: Hypothyroidism is treated with levothyroxine replacement and has no connection to androgen therapy or gonadotropin suppression.
w.Hyperemesis gravidarum: Hyperemesis is managed with fluids and antiemetics, and danazol is contraindicated in pregnancy because it virilizes a female fetus.
